idiom_name: for ... range with append (or hand-written generic helpers)
implementation_notes: Go deliberately ships no map/filter/reduce: the pipeline is realised as a for ... range loop that builds the result, with one loop per concern or one loop fusing several. Since generics (Go 1.18) a team can hand-write Map/Filter/Reduce helpers over []T, and the slices/maps packages provide the surrounding vocabulary (sorting, searching, cloning, iterating) but no map/filter - so the full structure is written by hand. The Go blog's own assessment of the iterator style is that 'in many cases a loop will be clearer'; keep loops as the default and introduce a helper only when the same stage recurs across the codebase.
pitfalls: append inside a loop reallocates as the slice grows: pre-size with make([]T, 0, len(src)), count survivors first, or use slices.Grow when the size is unknown.

Error-returning element functions do not compose: a stage that can fail forces the error out of the loop body, so either collect errors alongside the result or keep the explicit loop instead of a helper chain.

variants.name: iter.Seq push-iterator pipeline (range-over-func)
variants.idiom_name: iter.Seq[T] stages composed with range-over-func, materialised with slices.Collect
variants.implementation_notes: Go 1.23 makes lazy pipelines expressible: a stage is a function taking an iter.Seq[T] and returning another one (the Go blog's Filter example), the for-range statement accepts such functions, and the standard library supplies the ends - maps.Values/maps.Keys, slices.Values, slices.Collect, slices.Sorted. The blog's composition slices.Collect(Filter(isLong, maps.Values(m))) is a lazy stage chain over a map with a materialising terminal, and it works with any container type without changing the stages. The compiler turns the loop body into the yield function (push iterators are cheap and inline); iter.Pull is the escape hatch for lockstep consumption and costs a runtime coroutine per sequence. Choose this form when a stage chain is genuinely reused across container types; keep the loop otherwise.
pitfalls: Ignoring the yield contract is the classic bug: yield returns false when the consumer stopped, so a stage that does not check it cannot be broken out of (and a later yield panics).
iter.Pull starts a runtime coroutine: forgetting defer stop() leaks it, and pull iteration is measurably slower per element than push iteration.
Iterator chains make allocation and control flow less obvious than a loop; only the reuse across container types pays for the indirection.
